topic: The Magic of e: The Self-Replicating Function in Calculus
target_audience: Advanced high school students and first-year university students

sections.title: The Growth Paradox: A Rabbit Population
sections.content: Introduce the concept of exponential growth using a visual example. Explain that in many natural systems, the more you have, the faster you grow. This sets the stage for why we need a special base for these functions.
sections.example: An animation of a single 'Cyber-Rabbit' that splits into two. As the population grows, the 'speed' of reproduction increases proportionally to the number of rabbits currently on screen.

sections.title: Prerequisite Knowledge: Slopes and Derivatives
sections.content: Briefly review that the derivative (dy/dx) represents the slope of a tangent line at any point. Show a simple power function to contrast with what's coming next.
sections.example: A visual of a car driving up a hill (y = x^2). At any point, the 'steepness' of the hill is the derivative (2x).

sections.title: The Search for the Perfect Base
sections.content: Compare the derivatives of different exponential bases like 2^x and 3^x. Visually demonstrate that the slope of 2^x is always a bit less than its height, while the slope of 3^x is a bit more than its height.
sections.example: A split-screen graph showing y = 2^x and y = 3^x. At x=0, the slope of 2^x is ~0.69, while the slope of 3^x is ~1.10. We are looking for the 'Goldilocks' base where the slope equals exactly 1.

sections.title: Defining Euler's Number (e)
sections.content: Introduce e (approx. 2.718) as the unique number that satisfies the condition where the rate of change is exactly equal to the function's value. Define the identity: d/dx(e^x) = e^x.
sections.example: A 'Magic Growth Dial' that turns between 2 and 3. When it hits 2.718, the height of the curve and the slope of the tangent line become perfectly synchronized in length.

sections.title: Visualizing the 'Invariant' Property
sections.content: Use dynamic graphing to show that for the function f(x) = e^x, the y-value and the slope are identical at every single point. This is the 'holy grail' of calculus because it simplifies calculations.
sections.example: An animation where a point moves along the curve y = e^x. Two vertical bars appear: one measuring 'Height' and one measuring 'Steepness.' They stay exactly the same level throughout the movement.

sections.title: Application: The Cooling Effect
sections.content: Apply e to a real-world scenario using Newton's Law of Cooling. Explain how exponential functions with e describe how things return to equilibrium.
sections.example: A hot cup of coffee in a cold room. The rate at which the coffee cools (the 'slope' of the temperature) is proportional to the current temperature difference, modeled by an e^-t curve.

sections.title: Summary and Conclusion
sections.content: Recap that e is not just a random number, but the 'natural' base of growth where the function is its own derivative. This makes it the cornerstone of modeling change in physics, biology, and finance.
sections.example: A final collage showing the Cyber-Rabbit, the Cooling Coffee, and the e^x graph merging into the symbol 'e'.
